analysis.one_liner: Raises Pell Grants, caps student loan payments by income, and tightens rules on for-profit colleges.
analysis.headline: The House Education and Labor Committee approved the bill 28-22 on party lines, but the full House never voted on it before the Congress ended on January 3, 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The College Affordability Act would rewrite the main federal higher education law. It would raise the maximum Pell Grant for low-income students, pay states to hold down public college tuition, create tuition waivers through a federal-state partnership, and replace the tangle of student loan repayment plans with one income-based plan and one fixed plan. It would also expand loan forgiveness for public servants and impose new financial accountability rules on for-profit colleges, including a debt-to-earnings test that could cut off federal aid to poorly performing programs. The committee approved it near the end of 2020, but the House never brought it to the floor.
analysis.who_benefits: Low-income students get larger Pell Grants and simpler aid applications. Student loan borrowers get lower monthly payments under a single income-based plan and stronger access to public service loan forgiveness. Foster youth and homeless youth get in-state tuition. Students at career training programs get debt-to-earnings disclosures and protection from programs that leave graduates with debt they cannot repay.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Low-income students and student loan borrowers

how_it_helps.text: Increases the maximum federal Pell Grant award and makes permanent funding for minority-serving institutions, including historically Black colleges.
Replaces existing loan repayment plans with one income-based plan and one fixed plan, and lets existing borrowers switch to the new plans to lower their payments.
Expands public service loan forgiveness programs and creates appeal processes for borrowers whose forgiveness applications were denied.
Requires career training programs to meet debt-to-earnings performance metrics and publicly disclose graduate outcomes, or lose eligibility for federal student aid.
Creates a federal-state partnership with tuition waivers and a student success fund to lower the cost of public college attendance.
Grants in-state tuition rates to homeless youth and foster care youth, and extends Pell eligibility to children of Iraq and Afghanistan veterans.
Simplifies the FAFSA financial aid application and bars the Education Department from issuing rules that weaken Title IX sex discrimination enforcement.

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers fund the larger Pell Grants, the state incentives, and the new federal-state tuition partnership. For-profit colleges that rely heavily on federal aid risk losing access to those funds if graduates' debt-to-earnings rates fail the new tests. Loan servicers face a common manual, tighter oversight by the Education Department, and fewer repayment plan options to administer.
analysis.who_pays_short: Taxpayers, for-profit colleges, and loan servicers

drawbacks.text: The bill authorizes large new federal spending on Pell Grants, state incentives, and tuition waivers without an offset in the bill text, so the cost falls on taxpayers.
Extends federal student aid eligibility to certain noncitizen students, a provision that was contested by opponents of the bill.
The accountability rules focus heavily on for-profit colleges; critics argued that public and nonprofit institutions with poor outcomes face lighter consequences under the same framework.

Some programs, like the universal net price calculator and student data system, depend on future Education Department rulemaking and consumer testing, so their real-world effect would depend on later implementation.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For low-income students and borrowers, the gains are concrete: larger grants, lower payments, and disclosure rules that expose programs with poor outcomes. The costs are real but mostly fiscal — more federal spending on aid and grants — and the main structural criticism is that the accountability rules bite hardest on the for-profit sector while asking less of public institutions. On balance the bill would have shifted costs from individual students and borrowers to the federal treasury and forced poorly performing training programs to compete for aid.

outcome.mechanism: The House Education and Labor Committee approved the bill on a party-line vote near the end of 2020, but with only days left in the Congress the House leadership never brought it to the floor, and the Senate never took it up at all.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on October 15, 2019 by Rep. Bobby Scott, chairman of the House Committee on Education and Labor, and referred to that committee.
The committee held markup sessions on October 29 and 30, 2019, and voted 28-22 to order the bill reported as amended.
All 158 cosponsors were House Democrats; no House Republican signed on.
The committee did not report the bill until December 28, 2020 — the final days of the 116th Congress — when it was placed on the Union Calendar, the waiting list for House floor action.
No House floor vote was ever held, and the Senate took no action on the bill before the Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died without a vote, current borrowers kept the existing patchwork of repayment plans and no one received the expanded Pell Grants or tuition waivers. For-profit colleges kept operating under the pre-2014 status quo without a gainful employment debt-to-earnings test, and the federal government avoided the bill's new multi-billion-dollar spending commitments.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Borrowers kept the status quo; for-profit colleges kept light rules

sides.party_line_note: Every one of the 158 cosponsors was a House Democrat, and the committee's vote to report the bill was 28-22, with Republicans supplying all the no votes.

industries.note: Career training programs would have to meet debt-to-earnings metrics and disclose graduate outcomes, and proprietary schools would need at least 15% of revenue from non-federal sources, on pain of losing federal student aid. The bill also restricts for-profit institutions from converting to nonprofit status to escape oversight.

Servicers would operate under a single common manual and face oversight by the Education Department rather than the student aid office, while the consolidation of repayment plans would shrink the product lines they administer.
The bill would let borrowers refinance private student loans into federal loans, giving borrowers an exit from higher-rate private debt.

The bill would provide incentives for states to fund public institutions, make funding for historically Black and other minority-serving institutions permanent, and create a federal-state partnership with tuition waivers — new public money flowing directly to these schools.
